```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

## The ABC of Computational Text Analysis

Before we start we load and potentially install the packages we will use.
```{r}
install.packages("quanteda")
library(quanteda)
```


Step 1: We first need a text.
```{r}
seminar_description <- "Politics is about conflict and cooperation between societal groups. Harold Lasswell once defined it as “who gets what, when, how?”. Actors in the political arena, be it politicians, lobbyists, or mass movements, engage in (distributional) conflicts through language — be it spoken out loud in speeches, dialogues, and protest chants, or written down in position papers, protocols, and regulations. Throughout the seminar, students will learn how to use computational methods to explore the traces of conflict and cooperation preceding political change.We will focus on a policy field that not only affects every university student personally but also one that has been at the forefront of global change: Education. Over the past century, education has expanded from being a privilege of the few to an almost universal and global experience. In Europe, this trend is now increasingly leading to educational upgrading and a massive expansion of higher education. But how has this quiet revolution come about? And what are the central conflicts of educational governance today? The seminar is organized in three stages of the learning process. First, students will learn about the foundations of text-as-data in political science, as well as central theories of education politics. Further, they will study how to manually analyze texts without computational assistance. Next, we will focus on the methods of computational text analysis. Students will learn about the theoretical underpinnings of computational text analysis as well as the use of text-as-data methods through hands-on exercises using the R statistical programming language. We will also discuss recent examples of empirical research using computational text analysis. Last but not least, students will apply the learned methods in an in-class project. Small groups of students will be provided with textual data on a policy process and subsequently implement one or several of the techniques learned throughout the seminar"

```

### Note how the test is assigned a name through stateing the name, followed by "<-", and then including the text framed by "".


Step 2: We need to separate the text into its features.To safe the list of features (tokens) we can assign it an own name so we can work with it in further steps.
```{r}

seminar_toks <- tokens(seminar_description)

tokens(seminar_description)

```


Step 3: We can organise the features in a document-feature-matrix (dfm) which will also give us the frequency of each feature. 
```{r}
seminar_dfm <- dfm(seminar_toks)

dfm(seminar_toks)
```


Step 4: We can learn about the most used features using the **topfeatures** function drawing on the document-feature-matrix we have created. 
```{r}
topfeatures(seminar_dfm)
```
Alternative step 4: We can also combine several steps by using the "%>%" connector. Here we create a dfm from the tokens we have created (list of features [= mostly words]) and then we also directly ask it to print the topfeatures (= the most frequent features).
```{r}
dfm(seminar_toks) %>% topfeatures()

```


This analysis usually include several texts.
```{r}
grimmer <- c(" Language is everywhere in social life. Laws are written down, beliefs are articulated, and historical events are reported in words. Citizens complain to their representatives, organizers call people to protest, and advertisers try to sell products, all through language. Yet quantitative social science used texts surprisingly little until recently.The reason was practical. Collecting and transcribing everything people had written or said was hard. Reading collections with billions of words was impossible for any team, and sorting such texts into meaningful categories or measuring concepts in them seemed out of reach. So texts were used in small datasets or by large, well-funded teams. This has changed dramatically. The internet made texts much easier to acquire, computing power grew until a laptop could handle what once required a server, and methods were developed first in computer science and computational linguistics, then in the social sciences and humanities. Today it is common to see studies built on millions of social media messages or more books than any physical library holds. Most of these methods come from computer science, which brings a risk. Computer scientists are often interested in information retrieval, recommendation systems or benchmark tasks. Social scientists use text as data to learn about phenomena such as politics, literature or history. If we copy the default practices for selecting, evaluating and validating models from computer science without reflection, we can end up with unintended consequences. The book therefore treats text as data for social science tasks. It organizes these around four core tasks. Discovery is creating new concepts or ways of organizing the world. Measurement connects concepts to data, so we can describe how common something is. Causal inference uses such measures to ask what effect an intervention had. Prediction uses them to forecast values in the future. The usual machine learning distinction between supervised and unsupervised methods can obscure how these tools serve such tasks. The authors also stress that research should be sequential, iterative and inductive. We refine concepts and measurements as we see new data, confirm earlier results, test new hypotheses and generate hypotheses for future work. This happens across a community of researchers, not within a single study.A central example is Amy Catalinac’s work on Japan. She asked why politicians paid more attention to national security after 1997. She argued that a 1994 electoral reform changed their incentives: under the old multi-member districts, candidates from the same party competed by delivering local benefits, whereas the new system rewarded party platforms and national issues. She transcribed 7,497 candidate manifestos by hand, used a topic model to discover what they discussed, validated the topics by reading them and checking them against known facts about Japanese politics, and then tested her causal claim while ruling out alternative explanations.The lesson is that for social scientists, validation means checking whether a model’s output measures a concept well, not whether it predicts unseen words.")

```


### And now you: Conduct steps 2-4 on the "objectives" text
```{r}
toks_grimmer <- tokens(grimmer)
dfm_grimmer <- dfm(toks_grimmer) 
dfm(toks_grimmer) %>% topfeatures()
```
